title: McDonald’s Built a 515-Page Dossier on Me. It Says I’ll Never Stop Eating There
gist: A California data-access request to McDonald's returned a 515-page file showing the loyalty program maintains per-customer forward-looking forecasts — 2.16 predicted visits over six weeks, $13.49 average order, $29.15 total spend, an attrition likelihood of 0, an undefined 'CV2' value tier, occasion archetypes, and an RFM-ranked top-10 product list. Privacy experts interviewed say this depth is not unusual but standard practice for large American loyalty programs, and that the 515-page disclosure format itself defeats the transparency it is supposed to provide.

themes.theme: Loyalty programs run per-customer CLV models

insights.claim: McDonald's stores forward-looking predictions per individual customer, not just transaction history: an estimated 2.16 visits over the next six weeks, an estimated $13.49 average order spend, and an estimated $29.15 total spend — an individual-level customer lifetime value forecast maintained as a stored data field.
insights.speaker: Reece Rogers
insights.so_what: QSR loyalty data is a forecasting asset, not a marketing list — the same per-customer spend projections that feed promotional targeting could feed same-store-sales guidance.
insights.locator: While the sheer amount of data McDonald’s stored over the years

insights.claim: The dossier includes a 'Customer Attrition Likelihood' score — reported as 0 for this customer — showing that churn probability is computed and retained at the individual level in a fast-food loyalty program.
insights.speaker: Reece Rogers
insights.so_what: Per-customer churn scoring means promotional spend can be withheld from locked-in customers and concentrated on flight risks — a margin lever invisible in headline discount metrics.

insights.claim: Customers are sorted into undisclosed internal value tiers — the report lists a 'Customer Group Based on Historical Transactions' of CV2 with no explanation of what the tier means — so the classification driving treatment is opaque even under a legal data-access request.
insights.speaker: Reece Rogers
insights.so_what: Access rights deliver the value of a field without its meaning, which is the practical limit of current US transparency law and the gap the next round of rules will target.
insights.locator: Customer Group Based on Historical Transactions

insights.claim: McDonald's segments by consumption occasion rather than demographics, labeling this customer's behavioral archetypes as 'Food-Led Afternoon Snack' and 'On the Go Lunch in a Rush' based on past order patterns.
insights.speaker: Reece Rogers
insights.so_what: Occasion-based segmentation is the actual unit of QSR merchandising — daypart strategy and menu innovation are being driven off these labels, not off age or income cohorts.

insights.claim: The system applies classic recency-frequency-monetary math to the menu, deriving a top product (Large Diet Coke) and top product category (Wraps–Chicken) and maintaining a ranked top-10 relevance list spanning snack wraps, McShaker Fries, a Quarter Pounder, and 20-piece McNuggets.
insights.speaker: Reece Rogers
insights.so_what: An item-level relevance ranking per customer is the infrastructure for personalized pricing and LTO push — watch it show up as promotional efficiency in restaurant-level margins.
insights.locator: 10 Products McDonald's Ranks as Most Relevant to Me

insights.claim: Every app interaction generates a granular record of when, where, and what was purchased, including geographic concentration (San Francisco and Santa Barbara, 61 visits) and each scan of a Monopoly sweepstakes code along with the prize received.
insights.speaker: Reece Rogers
insights.so_what: Gamified promotions like Monopoly double as high-frequency location and identity capture events, which is a large part of why they persist despite the prize cost.
insights.locator: Much of my data report contains a detailed account

themes.theme: Surveillance as the core business model

insights.claim: The executive director of the Center for Digital Democracy characterizes McDonald's competitive advantage as commercial surveillance rather than food, reframing a restaurant chain as a data business.
insights.speaker: Jeff Chester
insights.so_what: If loyalty data is the durable asset, the right comparison set for QSR incumbents includes retail media networks — and so does the regulatory risk.
insights.quote: McDonald's secret sauce is really commercial surveillance,
insights.locator: When customers sign up for loyalty programs

insights.claim: Privacy experts told the reporter that this level of predictive detail, however invasive it feels, is fairly standard for how large American companies run loyalty programs — making it a sector-wide practice rather than a McDonald's outlier.
insights.speaker: Reece Rogers
insights.so_what: Any regulatory or litigation shock lands across the entire loyalty-program-dependent retail and restaurant complex, not on one brand.
insights.locator: Privacy experts I spoke with said this level of detail

insights.claim: McDonald's defends the practice in standard industry terms, saying it uses information such as past purchases to deliver a more engaging, personal experience with the most relevant deals, offers, and messages — the same justification every loyalty operator offers.
insights.speaker: Reece Rogers
insights.so_what: The uniformity of the industry defense signals a coordinated posture that will hold until a specific enforcement action forces differentiation.
insights.quote: Like many digital loyalty programs, we use information such as past purchases to provide a more engaging, personal customer experience—like delivering the most relevant deals, offers and messages.
insights.locator: McDonald's takes data privacy and security seriously

insights.claim: The director of Carnegie Mellon's CyLab Security and Privacy Institute argues that a 500-page disclosure is a wake-up call but is not in a format people can readily understand, and that the useful intervention would be highly detailed disclosures at sign-up specifying what enters the permanent record and what inferences will be drawn from it.
insights.speaker: Lorrie Cranor
insights.so_what: Access-request rights impose compliance cost without changing behavior; point-of-signup inference disclosure is the design that would actually bite, and it is where regulation is heading.
insights.quote: But it's not in a format that people will readily understand.
insights.locator: The 500 pages is kind of a wake-up call

insights.claim: Parsing the disclosure required using a generative AI tool to extract key information before verifying details against the original document — the volume of a compliant response is itself the barrier to comprehension.
insights.speaker: Reece Rogers
insights.so_what: Exercising data rights now practically requires AI tooling, which quietly raises the bar for who can hold data collectors accountable.
insights.locator: It was lengthy and difficult to parse

insights.claim: A University of Washington tech policy professor frames the core issue as structural power asymmetry: the consumer is mediated by the company's technology at the drive-through, kiosk, and app, inside an ecosystem designed by credentialed specialists to maximize profit.
insights.speaker: Ryan Calo
insights.so_what: The asymmetry framing supports treating loyalty programs as long-term surveillance rather than voluntary exchange — the legal theory that would expand liability beyond notice-and-consent.
insights.quote: You're in their ecosystem, and they have a bunch of people with letters after their names trying to design it in a way that maximizes profit.

insights.claim: A UC Irvine law professor argues the harm comes from aggregation rather than any single field: individually innocuous facts about what you eat or which musician you like, once collected over years and processed through AI, produce invasive knowledge of when you will be somewhere and what you do during the day.
insights.speaker: Ari Ezra Waldman
insights.so_what: If aggregation is the harm, per-field consent frameworks cannot address it — the liability attaches to the model, which is a much larger exposure for data-rich retailers.
insights.quote: the aggregation and collection of this information, as well as its processing through AI, can create pretty invasive and personal information about when you're going to be there, what you do during the day, and so forth,
insights.locator: While many of the data points in my McDonald’s report

insights.claim: The reporter exercised California deletion rights after the disclosure and resolved to stop patronizing the chain specifically to falsify its zero-attrition prediction — an illustration that publishing predictive scores to the subject can itself change the behavior being predicted.
insights.speaker: Reece Rogers
insights.so_what: Mandated disclosure of predictive scores creates a feedback loop that degrades the model — a real, underrated cost to firms of expanding access rights.
insights.quote: I want to leave it all behind just to prove the algorithm wrong.
insights.locator: Along with the right to request access to the data collected about me
